'''''Eucalyptus cinerea''''', commonly known as the '''Argyle apple''', '''mealy stringbark'''<ref name="CANBR">{{cite web |title=''Eucalyptus cinerea'' subsp. ''cinerea''|url=https://apps.lucidcentral.org/euclid/text/entities/eucalyptus_cinerea_subsp._cinerea.htm|publisher=Euclid: Centre for Australian National Biodiversity Research |access-date=4 June 2020}}</ref> or '''silver dollar tree''',<ref>{{cite book |title=''The New Sunset Western Garden Book'' |page=311 |publisher=Sunset Publishing |date=2012 |isbn=978-0-376-03920-0}}</ref> is a species of small- to medium-sized tree that is [[Endemism|endemic]] to south-eastern [[Australia]]. It has rough, fibrous bark on the trunk and branches, usually only juvenile, [[wikt:glaucous#Adjective|glaucous]], egg-shaped evergreen leaves, flower buds in groups of three, white flowers and conical to bell-shaped fruit.[[File:Eucalyptus cinerea leaves.jpg|thumb|Leaves, buds, flowers and fruit]]

==Description==
''Eucalyptus cinerea'' is a tree that typically grows to a height of {{cvt|15-30|m}} tall and forms a [[lignotuber]]. It has thick, fibrous, reddish brown to grey brown, longitudinally fissured bark on the trunk to the small branches. The leaves on young plants and on [[coppice]] regrowth are arranged in opposite pairs, [[Sessility (botany)|sessile]], glaucous, broadly egg-shaped to more or less round, up to {{cvt|80|mm}} long and {{cvt|50|mm}} wide. Intermediate leaves are arranged in opposite pairs, glaucous, egg-shaped to lance-shaped, {{cvt|48-90|mm}} long and {{cvt|20-45|mm}} wide on a [[Petiole (botany)|petiole]] {{cvt|4-15|mm}} long. Adult leaves are arranged alternately, lance-shaped, {{cvt|90-140|mm}} long and {{cvt|15-50|mm}} wide on a [[Petiole (botany)|petiole]] up to {{cvt|11|mm}} long. The flower buds are arranged in groups of three in leaf [[wikt:axil|axil]]s on a [[Peduncle (botany)|peduncle]] {{cvt|2-9|mm}} long, the individual buds sessile or on a [[Pedicel (botany)|pedicel]] up to {{cvt|3|mm}} long. Mature buds are glaucous, diamond-shaped, {{cvt|6-8|mm}} long and {{cvt|3-5|mm}} wide with a conical [[Operculum (botany)|operculum]]. Flowering occurs between May and November and the flowers are white. The fruit is a woody, conical to bell-shaped [[Capsule (botany)|capsule]] {{cvt|4-7|mm}} long and {{cvt|5-9|mm}} wide with the valves level with the rim or slightly beyond.<ref name="CANBR" /><ref name="RBGS">{{cite web |last1=Hill |first1=Ken |title=''Eucalyptus cinerea'' |url=http://plantnet.rbgsyd.nsw.gov.au/cgi-bin/NSWfl.pl?page=nswfl&lvl=sp&name=Eucalyptus~cinerea |publisher=Royal Botanic Garden Sydney |access-date=30 April 2019}}</ref><ref name="RBGV">{{cite web|author-link1=Ian Brooker |last1=Brooker |first1=M. Ian |last2=Slee |first2=Andrew V. |title=''Eucalyptus cinerea'' subsp. ''victoriensis'' |url=https://vicflora.rbg.vic.gov.au/flora/taxon/c2ff4987-3827-45b7-8fb6-2315baff8ef1 |publisher=Royal Botanic Gardens Victoria |access-date=30 April 2019}}</ref><ref name="ABRS">{{cite web |last1=Chippendale |first1=George M. |title=''Eucalyptus cinerea'' |url=https://profiles.ala.org.au/opus/foa/profile/Eucalyptus%20cinerea |publisher=Australian Biological Resources Study, Department of the Environment and Energy, Canberra |access-date=30 April 2019}}</ref><ref name=Brooker>{{cite book|author1=Brooker, I.|author-link1=Ian Brooker| author2= Kleinig, D.|title=Eucalyptus, An illustrated guide to identification|publisher= Reed Books|location= Melbourne|date= 1996}}</ref>

==Taxonomy and naming==
''Eucalyptus cinerea'' was first formally described by the botanist [[George Bentham]] in 1867 from the [[herbarium]] of [[Ferdinand von Mueller]], and the description was published in ''[[Flora Australiensis]]''.<ref name=APNI>{{cite web|title=''Eucalyptus cinerea''|url= https://id.biodiversity.org.au/instance/apni/455988|publisher=APNI|access-date=30 April 2019}}</ref><ref name="Benth.">{{cite book|author-link1=George Bentham |last1=Bentham |first1=George|author-link2=Ferdinand von Mueller |last2=von Mueller |first2=Ferdinand |title=Flora Australiensis (Volume 3) |date=1867 |volume=3 |publisher=Lovell Reeve & Co. |location=London |page=239 |url=https://www.biodiversitylibrary.org/item/41807#page/247/mode/1up |access-date=30 April 2019}}</ref> The [[Botanical name|specific epithet]] (''cinerea'') is a [[Latin]] word meaning "ash-coloured" or "grey"<ref name="RWB">{{cite book|author-link1=Roland W. Brown|last1=Brown|first1=Roland Wilbur|title=The Composition of Scientific Words|date=1956|publisher=Smithsonian Institution Press|location=Washington, D.C.|page=204}}</ref> referring to the white, waxy bloom on the foliage, buds and fruit of this species.<ref name="CANBR" />

Two subspecies of ''E. cinerea'' have been described and the names accepted by the [[Australian Plant Census]]:<ref name="ASB">{{cite journal|author-link1=Ian Brooker |last1=Brooker |first1=M. Ian H. |last2=Slee |first2=Andrew V. |last3=Briggs |first3=John D. |title=A taxonomic revision of ''Eucalyptus'' ser. ''Argyrophyllae'' |journal=Australian Systematic Botany |date=1995 |volume=8 |issue=4 |page=507 |doi=10.1071/SB9950499}}</ref>
* ''Eucalyptus cinerea'' subsp. ''cinerea''<ref name=APC1>{{cite web|title=''Eucalyptus cinerea'' subsp. ''cinerea''|url= https://biodiversity.org.au/nsl/services/apc-format/display/203853|publisher=Australian Plant Census|access-date=30 April 2019}}</ref> has a [[Crown (botany)|crown]] of mostly juvenile leaves and grows in woodland between [[Sofala, New South Wales|Sofala]] and [[Tumut]] in [[New South Wales]];<ref name="RBGS" />
* ''Eucalyptus cinerea'' subsp. ''triplex''<ref name=APC2>{{cite web|title=''Eucalyptus cinerea'' subsp. ''triplex''|url= https://biodiversity.org.au/nsl/services/apc-format/display/119684|publisher=Australian Plant Census|access-date=30 April 2019}}</ref> has a crown with both juvenile and intermediate leaves; and occurs in the [[Australian Capital Territory]] and [[Captains Flat]] in New South Wales.<ref name="RBGS" />

A third subspecies, subspecies ''victoriensis'' was described in 2018. It is the tallest subspecies and has adult leaves in its crown.<ref name="RBGV" /><ref name="Rule">{{cite journal|author-link1=Kevin James Rule |last1=Rule |first1=Kevin J.|author-link2=Neville Grant Walsh |last2=Walsh |first2=Neville G. |title=Two new subspecific taxa with the ''Eucalyptus'' Series ''Argyrophyllae'' for Victoria |journal=Muelleria |date=2018 |volume=8 |issue=4 |pages=87–90 |url=https://www.rbg.vic.gov.au/documents/Muelleria_Vol_36_-_pp81-91_Rule_and_Walsh_-_FINAL_WEB.pdf |access-date=30 April 2019}}</ref>

The [[Wiradjuri]] people of [[New South Wales]] use the name ''gundhay'' for the species.<ref name=wpu>{{cite book |editor1-last=Williams |editor1-first=Alice |editor2-last=Sides |editor2-first=Tim |date=2008 |title=Wiradjuri Plant Use in the Murrumbidgee Catchment |publisher=Murrumbidgee Catchment Management Authority |page=27 |isbn=0 7347 5856 1}}</ref>

==Distribution and habitat==
Argyle apple is typically found from north of [[Bathurst, New South Wales|Bathurst]] (33° S), in central west [[New South Wales]], to the [[Beechworth]] area of [[Victoria (Australia)|Victoria]] (36° S).<ref name=Brooker/> It is often part of grassy or sclerophyll woodland communities growing in  shallow and relatively infertile soils usually as part of the understorey. Subspecies ''cinerea'' occurs in the [[Australian Capital Territory]] and [[Captains Flat]] in New South Wales and subspecies ''triplex'' in the [[Australian Capital Territory]] and [[Captains Flat]] in New South Wales.<ref name="RBGS" /> Subspecies ''victoriensis'' is only known from hilly country near [[Beechworth]] in [[Victoria (Australia)|Victoria]].<ref name="RBGV" />

==Uses==
[[File:Eucalyptus cinerea street trees Henty St.jpg|thumb|Trees on both sides of a street in inner Canberra]]
===Aboriginal uses===
The Wiradjuri people of NSW use the bark and timber of the species to make tools, string and rope, shelters and to make fire.<ref name=wpu/>
===Horticultural uses===
''Eucalyptus cinerea'' is used as a park and street tree where it is planted widely in [[Canberra]].<ref>{{cite web |title=Design Standards for Urban Infrastructure - Plant Species for Urban Landscape Projects in Canberra: ''Eucalyptus cinerea'' (Eci) |url=https://www.cityservices.act.gov.au/__data/assets/pdf_file/0004/1502968/Eucalyptus-cinerea.pdf |website=Transport Canberra and City Services |publisher=ACT Government |access-date=12 May 2024}}</ref>
